messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 27
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Physical Therapist
- Trauma Type: Sexual assault
- Pcl5: 49

He is a 27-year-old Middle Eastern man who comes across as composed at first meeting, careful with his words and noticeably respectful in the way he speaks about others. He is married and works as a physical therapist, a role that once felt natural to him because he liked helping people use their bodies without pain. Before the assault, he describes himself as active, socially easygoing, and proud of being someone others relied on. He was the kind of person who stayed late to finish a patient’s treatment plan and did not mind the physical closeness that comes with his work.

The assault happens when he is still building the life he has imagined for himself. He does not describe it quickly; he circles it, pauses, and sometimes goes quiet for long stretches before continuing. The event is sexual in nature and leaves him feeling stunned, then deeply ashamed. In the hours afterward, he is less concerned with what happened than with the fact that it happened to him. He washes repeatedly, as if he can remove what he cannot bear to hold in memory. He avoids telling anyone right away, including his wife, because he cannot imagine how to put the experience into words without hearing himself sound weak or exposed. In his mind, he keeps returning to a single question: why did he not stop it, why did he not fight harder, why did he freeze.

In the weeks that follow, he becomes sharply aware of his own body in ways that feel foreign and threatening. Ordinary sensations can bring back the assault without warning. A smell, a certain tone of voice, being approached from behind, or a hand resting briefly on his shoulder can make his chest tighten and his stomach drop. At work, he begins to feel uneasy during treatments that require close physical contact. He still helps patients, but he monitors every movement more carefully, positioning himself so he can see the room, standing closer to the door, and avoiding situations where he might be alone with someone he does not know well. He notices that he is less patient than he used to be and more likely to feel irritated by small interruptions. He says he feels like he is always bracing for something to happen.

Sleep becomes one of the first things to change. He lies awake replaying the event in fragments, trying to make sense of what he remembers and what he wishes he could forget. When he does sleep, he wakes abruptly, disoriented and sweaty, with his heart racing. At times he dreams of being trapped, pinned down, or unable to speak. He begins to dread bedtime because it means surrendering to the possibility of those images returning. During the day, he feels pulled back into the memory by sudden flashes that seem to come without invitation. He can be in the middle of a session with a patient, explaining an exercise or adjusting posture, and then realize he has lost track of what he was saying because his mind has wandered to the assault.

He and his wife have known each other long enough that she notices the change before he can explain it. He becomes more distant, less affectionate, and more defensive when she asks what is wrong. He wants comfort but feels panicked by closeness, especially when it is unexpected. He worries that if he tells her everything, she will see him differently, or that he will burden her with something she cannot fix. At the same time, hiding it makes him feel isolated and alone in his own marriage. The shame is persistent and corrosive; he often interprets his reactions as evidence that something is wrong with him rather than as the aftereffects of what was done to him.

Over time, he starts to avoid certain places and routines that remind him of the assault. He changes the routes he takes, declines social invitations more often, and is more careful about where he sits in public. He stays busy, partly because work gives him structure and partly because slowing down leaves too much room for intrusive memories. Even so, he feels less present in his life than he used to. He describes himself as functioning on the outside while internally feeling as if he is always scanning for danger. In session, he speaks about wanting to return to the person he was before the assault, but also recognizing that he is no longer able to move through the world with the same ease.
